questions.question: What are attr_accessor and friends in Ruby?
questions.title: attr_accessor and Friends
questions.direct_answer: `attr_accessor` generates getters and setters for instance variables: `attr_accessor :name` creates `name` (getter) and `name=` (setter). `attr_reader` = getter only (read-only); `attr_writer` = setter only (write-only); `attr_accessor` = both. They're meta-programming — Ruby defines the methods for you: def name; @name; end; def name=(v); @name = v; end is what attr_accessor :name expands to. Instance variables (@name) are private by default; attr_* exposes them. Use attr_reader by default (don't expose setters you don't need); use attr_accessor only when both make sense. You can pass multiple names: attr_accessor :name, :age. They're not fields — they're method definitions; you can override them later in the class if you need custom logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know attr_reader (getter), attr_writer (setter), attr_accessor (both), and that they generate methods from instance variables.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Over-exposing with attr_accessor when attr_reader would do (don't expose setters you don't need).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: attr_accessor = getter + setter; attr_reader = getter only; attr_writer = setter only. Generate methods from @vars. Prefer attr_reader by default.

sections.title: Getters and Setters
sections.content: attr_accessor generates getters and setters for instance variables: attr_accessor name creates name (getter) and name equals (setter). attr_reader equals getter only (read-only); attr_writer equals setter only (write-only); attr_accessor equals both. They're meta-programming — Ruby defines the methods for you: def name; name var; def name equals v; name var equals v; end is what attr_accessor name expands to. Instance variables (name var) are private by default; attr star exposes them. Use attr_reader by default (don't expose setters you don't need); use attr_accessor only when both make sense. You can pass multiple names: attr_accessor name age. They're not fields — they're method definitions; you can override them later in the class if you need custom logic.

sections.title: attr_*
sections.content:
attr_reader=getter; attr_writer=setter; attr_accessor=both. Generate from @vars. Prefer attr_reader.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  R[attr_reader :name] --> G[name -> @name]
  W[attr_writer :name] --> S[name= -> @name=]
  A[attr_accessor :name] --> B[both]
```

sections.title: attr_accessor
sections.content:
```ruby
class Person
  attr_accessor :name, :age     # getter + setter for both
  attr_reader :id               # getter ONLY (read-only)
  attr_writer :secret           # setter ONLY (write-only)

  def initialize(id, name, age)
    @id, @name, @age = id, name, age
    @secret = nil
  end
end

p = Person.new(1, 'Ada', 30)

# attr_accessor :name, :age -> getter + setter
p.name            # 'Ada'  (getter)
p.name = 'Bob'    # setter
p.age = 31

# attr_reader :id -> getter only
p.id              # 1
# p.id = 2        # NoMethodError (no setter)

# attr_writer :secret -> setter only
p.secret = 'x'
# p.secret        # NoMethodError (no getter)

# What attr_accessor :name EXPANDS to:
#   def name;     @name; end   # getter
#   def name=(v); @name = v; end # setter

# Prefer attr_reader by default; add setters only when needed.
# Multiple names: attr_accessor :a, :b, :c
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Over-exposing with attr_accessor when attr_reader would do (don't add setters you don't need).
Forgetting instance vars (@x) are private by default (attr_* exposes them).
Thinking attr_* are fields — they're method definitions (you can override them).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: attr_accessor generates a getter + setter; attr_reader = getter only; attr_writer = setter only.
attr_accessor :name expands to def name; @name; end and def name=(v); @name = v; end.
Instance variables (@name) are private by default; attr_* exposes them.
Prefer attr_reader by default; add setters only when you need them.
